content:
The biggest wins for daily life with arthritis come from three habits. Spread demanding tasks across the day and week, use your largest and strongest joints rather than small ones, and use simple aids that take the strain. An NHS or council occupational therapist can assess you for free and suggest equipment and changes that suit your home.

Start the day gently

Morning stiffness is common, especially with inflammatory arthritis. Try:

  • a few gentle movements in bed before getting up, such as ankle circles, knee bends and finger stretches
  • a warm shower early in the day to loosen joints
  • laying out clothes the night before
  • timing painkillers, if you take them, so they are working when you get up. Ask your pharmacist how.

Related reading: Arthritis - How's Life Living With Arthritis?

Pace yourself

Pacing means doing a steady amount of activity every day rather than overdoing it on good days and paying for it afterwards. Break big jobs into smaller chunks. Alternate heavy and light tasks, and sit down for jobs that do not need you to stand. Plan rest before you need it, not after.

Protect your joints

  • carry bags over your forearm or shoulder, or use a trolley, instead of gripping with fingers
  • push open doors with your shoulder or hip rather than your hand
  • slide heavy pans along the worktop instead of lifting
  • use two hands to lift a mug or kettle
  • avoid staying in one position too long. Get up and move every 30 minutes.

In the kitchen

  • use lightweight pans and a kettle tipper
  • buy pre-chopped vegetables or frozen ingredients on bad days
  • try a perching stool so you can sit while preparing food
  • use jar openers, electric can openers and tap turners
  • cook in batches when you feel well and freeze portions

Washing and dressing

  • a long-handled sponge and a bath board or shower seat reduce reaching and bending
  • grab rails beside the toilet and bath make getting up safer
  • choose clothes with front fastenings, elastic waists and slip-on shoes with good grip
  • a long-handled shoe horn, sock aid and button hook help with stiff hips or hands

Housework and garden

  • spread housework across the week, one room a day
  • use long-handled dusters, lightweight vacuums and a grabber
  • raised beds and kneeling stools make gardening easier
  • keep frequently used items between shoulder and hip height

Getting out and about

Good walking shoes, a walking stick if needed and planned rest stops make outings easier. You may be eligible for a Blue Badge if walking is very difficult. Many supermarkets offer delivery, which can save energy for things you enjoy.

Equipment and adaptations

You can ask your council for a free needs assessment. This can lead to equipment such as rails, raised toilet seats or perching stools, and sometimes home adaptations. Equipment and minor adaptations costing less than £1,000 are usually free in England. Larger changes may be funded by a Disabled Facilities Grant.

Look after your energy and mood

Fatigue and low mood are common and real parts of arthritis. Good sleep habits, regular gentle exercise and staying in touch with friends all help. If you feel low most days, talk to your GP. NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referrals in England.

Keep moving

Exercise is a core treatment for arthritis according to NICE. Daily movement keeps joints flexible and muscles strong, which makes every other task easier. Even short walks or chair exercises count.

Small changes that add up

You do not need to change everything at once. Pick one area that frustrates you most, such as getting dressed or cooking, and try two or three ideas for a fortnight. Keep what helps and drop what does not. Write down tasks that leave you sore the next day, as these are the ones to break up or adapt.

Ask family and friends for help with specific jobs, such as changing the bed or carrying the shopping in. Accepting help with heavy jobs leaves you more energy for the things that matter to you.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
